methods.label: Reduce the intercept restrictions to divisors
methods.explanation:
Let the positive prime \(x\)-intercept be \(p\), and let the positive integer \(y\)-intercept be \(b\). Both intercepts are nonzero, so the line has equation
\[
\frac{x}{p}+\frac{y}{b}=1.
\]
Since it passes through \((4,3)\),
\[
\frac4p+\frac3b=1.
\]
The term \(3/b\) is positive, so \(4/p<1\), giving \(p>4\). We can therefore solve for \(b\) without dividing by zero:
\[
b=\frac{3p}{p-4}=3+\frac{12}{p-4}.
\]
This form makes the integer restriction useful: \(p-4\) must be a positive divisor of \(12\). Its complete list of possibilities is
\[
p-4\in\{1,2,3,4,6,12\},
\]
so
\[
p\in\{5,6,7,8,10,16\}.
\]
Only \(5\) and \(7\) are prime. They give \((p,b)=(5,15)\) and \((7,7)\), respectively. The corresponding lines satisfy
\[
\frac45+\frac3{15}=1,
\qquad
\frac47+\frac37=1.
\]
Every admissible line appears in the divisor search, and each intercept pair determines one line. The two different \(x\)-intercepts give distinct lines. Therefore there are \(\boxed{2}\) lines, choice C.
